title: Negative quantum friction in nanoscale water flows: the Wigner picture
authors: Adriano Tiribocchi, Marco Lauricella, Efthimios Kaxiras, Sauro Succi
abstract: We explore the phenomenon of "quantum" friction based on a single-particle model patterned after the Wigner equation describing electrons flow in a solid wall confining nanoscale water flows. The numerical simulations show a clear signature of negative quantum friction, namely a net momentum transfer from the electrons in the solid wall to the flowing water molecules. Such net momentum transfer results into a sizeable reduction of the water friction, up to forty percent, depending on the strength of the coupling between classical and quantum fluctuations. Our results offer the prospect of a theoretical framework bridging classical and quantum description by using continuum kinetic theories and particle-based simulations.
summary: This paper theoretically investigates how quantum effects modify friction in confined water flows by modeling electron interactions using the Wigner equation. Numerical simulations reveal a signature of negative quantum friction, which substantially reduces the drag force experienced by the liquid. This work establishes a theoretical bridge between continuum kinetic theories and particle dynamics for nanoscale energy transport.
main_problem: The study investigates the phenomenon of 'quantum' friction occurring during nanoscale water flows, specifically examining how quantum fluctuations modify energy dissipation.
main_result: Negative quantum friction is predicted and observed, leading to a significant reduction (up to 40%) in the frictional drag experienced by the flowing water compared to classical predictions.
method: The research employs numerical simulations solving a fractional Langevin equation derived from modeling electron dynamics using the Wigner picture.
model_or_system: The system models electrons moving in a solid wall confining nanoscale water flows, where interactions are mediated by charge fluctuations ('hydrons') in the liquid. The theory bridges continuum kinetic descriptions with particle-based simulations.
key_observables: Negative quantum friction (net momentum transfer from electrons to water), average current $\langle  ar{J} angle$, and force profiles ($F_{1/3}(x)$).
important_parameters: Quantumness parameter ($q$), fluctuation amplitude ($W$), and the degree of coupling between classical and quantum fluctuations.
main_assumptions: The analysis utilizes the Wigner formulation as an alternative to Keldysh formalism, and approximations include quasi-static updates for the potential $V(x)$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of current $J$ showing decay with increasing quantum parameters, quantifying the reduction in average current $\langle  ar{J} angle$, and displaying probability density functions of the fractional force components.
paper_structure: The paper builds a theoretical framework using the Wigner equation to model electron-water interaction. It then uses numerical simulations on a fractional Langevin equation to calculate observables, demonstrating how quantum effects manifest as negative friction coefficients that reduce drag.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics where quantum corrections significantly alter macroscopic transport properties (friction), offering insights into energy conversion at the nanoscale boundary between classical and quantum regimes.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) Schematic representation of the mechanisms driving the electronic current: hydrons (charged fluctuations of water molecules, red particles) transfer momentum to the electrons in the solid (black particles) through screened Coulomb interactions (black dotted line) and phonons (wavy lines), resulting from hits against the wall. (b) Schematic functioning of a hydronic generator. As the liquid flows through a nanotube connected to an external circuit, an electric current, caused by the hydroelectronic drag, results from the flow of the liquid. Figures adapted from Refs.[6, 7].

Figure 2. Time evolution of the current J of a single particle (extracted from N = 100 different realizations) for pϕ = 1, W = 0, 0.2 and q2 = 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03. The solid curve represents the deterministic case, without water fluctuations, whereby the particle is driven towards the steady state condi- tion p = pϕ on a time scale 1/γ (classical friction). Increasing q2 leads to larger amplitude fluctuations and a slight decrease of the average current.

Figure 3. Current vs q2, averaged over time (T = 20, 000) and realizations (N = 100) for different values of W and pϕ = 1. A net decrease of the electronic current at increasing q2 is visible, amounting to about 30 percent at q2 = 0.05 (semi-quantum) regime. The curve obeys a fit of the form J(q2) = J(0) −∆J(1 −exp(−q2/Q2)), with ∆J/J(0) ∼0.32 and Q2 ∼0.015 for W=0.2 (dashed curve), ∆J/J(0) ∼0.37 and Q2 ∼0.013 for W = 0.3 (dotted curve), ∆J/J(0) ∼0.4 and Q2 ∼0.009 for W = 0.4 (dot-dashed curve).

Figure 4. The probability density of F1 (a,b,c) and F1/3 (d,e,f) for pϕ = 0.1, W = 0.2 and q2 = 0.01, q2 = 0.03, q2 = 0.05. Regardless of the values of q2, F1 closely follows a Gaussian distribution where µ ∼0 and σ ∼0.1. By contrast, F1/3 shows a negative skewness, with an increasingly heavy left tail, as q2 augments, with the skewness approximately ranging from -0.3 for q2 = 0.01 to −0.4 for q2 = 0.05. We associate the progressive increase of negative skewness with the reduction of ⟨¯J⟩. In panel (g) we show the typical trend of ¯F1/3 over N = 100 realizations. Increasing q2 leads to a shift towards negative values with a concurrent increase of the fluctuation amplitude.

Figure 5. Time evolution of the current J of a single particle for different values of q2 and W = 0.1 (a,b), W = 0.3 (c,d), W = 0.4 (e,f). These ones are compared to the classical unperturbed case, where q2 = 0 and W = 0. The left column shows systems whose absolute value of the time averages is minimum among all realizations, while in the right column the time average is maximum. On a general basis, increasing q2 and W enhances the amplitude of the fluctuations, with a progressive shift towards values considerably lower than 1.
